title: Direct from the seed: an atomic resolution protein structure by ab initio MicroED

paper_content.abstract: While purifying the seed protein crambin, we find that needles of pure protein nanocrystals form spontaneously during the drying of a simple ethanolic purification drop. These needles diffract X-rays weakly but are well-suited for microcrystal electron diffraction (MicroED). Merging data from 58 such nanocrystals yields diffraction to 0.85 Å resolution and solves the structure ab initio using a five-residue helical fragment to initiate density modification. The resulting map enables automated model building and resolves individual hydrogen atoms. This work reports an atomic resolution MicroED structure of the protein crambin solved ab initio. This study establishes a publicly available benchmark showing that sub-ångström ab initio MicroED can be achieved on standard 200 kV instrumentation without energy filtering or FIB milling, when serial merging is combined with anisotropy aware truncation to address preferred orientation. For this dataset, isotropic truncation alone did not produce a fragment placement suitable for phasing in this workflow, whereas applying anisotropy correction supported an ab initio solution.
paper_content.introduction:
Crystallography, a cornerstone method for determining protein structures, has traditionally been limited by crystal size. X-ray crystallography, the gold standard for determining atomic resolution structures, requires relatively large, well-ordered crystals - typically tens to hundreds of micrometers across. Yet many proteins naturally form only extremely tiny crystals, far smaller than this threshold, leaving a significant fraction of important biological molecules structurally inaccessible. Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), another powerful approach, struggles to achieve high-resolution structures of proteins less than 100 kDa1. This limits its utility for many biologically important molecules, e.g., the median size of a human protein is only about 40 kDa2.

Microcrystal electron diffraction (MicroED) has emerged as an approach to overcome these limitations3. Instead of X-rays, MicroED uses electrons, which interact far more strongly with matter4. This interaction allows high-resolution structure determination from crystals thousands of times smaller by volume than those required for traditional X-ray methods. Although many crystals are invisible to the naked eye5 and often too small or delicate for standard crystallography, they can still yield atomic-resolution structures using MicroED. In favorable cases, direct analysis of nanocrystalline material is possible6,7.

Despite its promise, phasing protein structures by MicroED remains heavily reliant on pre-existing knowledge. Molecular replacement (MR) for MicroED, demonstrated with lysozyme in 2013–20148,9, is the workhorse method and has delivered important structures like Ca2+-ATPase10, R2lox11, MyD8812, and the human lens membrane protein MP2013. The arrival of AlphaFold214 has further expanded the reach of MR. However, this reliance on homologous models creates a fundamental limitation: it generates phase bias and leaves proteins with novel folds inaccessible. Establishing reliable ab initio phasing methods that remove this dependence is essential. While this has been routine for small-molecule electron crystallography for years6,15–17, progress for proteins has been incremental, moving from direct methods on small peptides18, to fragment-based searches19, and recently to density-modification-based bootstrapping from minimal ideal fragments20. Prior ab initio MicroED demonstrations established feasibility, and many implementations have operated in regimes that mitigate geometric incompleteness and anisotropy, for example, by reducing thickness or by using microscope and detector configurations that broaden the usable data range. Here, we ask whether an ab initio solution remains achievable on widely available 200 kV hardware without energy filtration or FIB milling, and we assess whether anisotropy-aware data treatment is a practical determinant of success in this dataset, a consideration that may be important in similarly anisotropic cases. Rather than introducing a new phasing algorithm, our goal is to provide a well-characterized, publicly available atomic resolution MicroED benchmark that complements existing lysozyme and proteinase K datasets and enables rigorous testing of electron-specific methods.

In this study, we bridge this methodological gap by using the classic benchmark protein crambin21. For decades, Crambin has served as a proving ground for the most advanced crystallographic methods. Its 1981 structure by Hendrickson and Teeter was a landmark in de novo phasing using sulfur anomalous scattering22, and it was later the protein solved by Hauptman and Weeks’ purely mathematical direct methods, a triumph developed at our home institutions23. Subsequent X-ray studies reached 0.48 Å24 and 0.54 Å25, and more recently, a 0.70 Å26 room-temperature X-ray structure provided an ultrahigh-resolution description of the crambin solvent network and disorder in the PL and SI isoforms. Furthermore, neutron diffraction has been reported to 1.1 Å resolution at room temperature27.

Despite this storied history in X-ray and neutron science, a completed de novo investigation of crambin by MicroED has remained unexplored. While a 1.07 Å MicroED structure solved by molecular replacement has been briefly described in a technical note (Rigaku Application note PX031)28, the full potential of using electrons to solve this benchmark protein from first principles has not been realized. We discovered that a simple ethanolic extraction from finely ground seeds spontaneously yields an abundant supply of nanocrystals ideal for such a test. Therefore, we set an ambitious goal: to determine if data from these naturally formed nanocrystals were of sufficient quality to not only break the sub-ångström barrier but to solve the structure ab initio from a minimal, non-homologous five-residue helical fragment29.

Here we report an electron ab initio structure of crambin at sub-ångström resolution obtained directly from spontaneously formed nanocrystals collected on standard 200 kV hardware without using a focused ion-beam to thin the crystals or an energy filter, with data merged from multiple crystals to mitigate preferred orientation. We position crambin as a reference for electron-specific methods and compare it with prior ab initio MicroED results.
paper_content.results:
At a tale of two crystals: swapping fortunes in X-ray and electron diffraction

Our investigation began with a serendipitous discovery. During a simple ethanolic extraction of crushed Crambe abyssinica seeds (Supplementary Fig. S1), we found that a 1 µL droplet of the protein-rich solution nucleated a dense shower of sub-micron, needle-shaped crystals within seconds as the solvent evaporated (Fig. 1A). These crystals formed without a separate screening step. These needles proved unsuitable for X-ray diffraction. A single 14 µm needle diffracted poorly, only reaching 1.6 Å resolution and suffered from rapid radiation decay (Supplementary Fig. S2, Supplementary Table S1). In contrast, they proved ideal for MicroED. When loaded into the TEM, we noticed many tiny rod-shaped crystals on the grid (Fig. 1B). High-resolution imaging of these crystals showed clear lattice lines (Fig. 1C) that contained information to 3.6 Å by analysis of the Fourier transform of these images (Fig. 1D). These crystals consistently diffracted electrons to high resolution (Fig. 1E).

We also grew large, block-like crystals using traditional vapor diffusion (Supplementary Fig. S3). These crystals exhibited the opposite behavior: they produced excellent X-ray diffraction to beyond 0.8 Å but were too thick for MicroED. We mechanically crushed these blocks to obtain fragments for MicroED, but the crushed fragments produced markedly inferior electron diffraction data compared to the spontaneously formed needles (Supplementary Fig. S4). For electrons, the limiting dimension is thickness along the beam (below twice the inelastic mean free path, or about 500 to 600 nm)30; most crushed fragments remained too thick, increasing dynamical scattering and absorption. This system-specific outcome contrasts with reports where crushed fragments diffracted well, such as De La Cruz et al.31, where fragmentation produced abundant electron-transparent crystals; here the spontaneous needles provided higher-quality MicroED data.

This inversion of crystal quality between the two diffraction methods motivated our collection strategy. Rather than rely on non-ideal fragments to randomize orientation, we tackled the preferred orientation problem of the spontaneously formed needles directly using a serial crystallography approach. By merging data from multiple crystals, we aimed to overcome geometric data loss inherent to a single orientation and build a complete, high-redundancy dataset.

Achieving an atomic-resolution microED dataset by overcoming anisotropy

Having established the superiority of the spontaneously formed nanocrystals for MicroED experiments, we proceeded with data collection. The primary technical hurdle was, as anticipated, the severe preferred orientation of the needles on the grid32. This morphology introduces a fundamental challenge for MicroED: diffraction quality is highest at low tilt angles, where the electron beam passes through the thinnest dimension of the crystal, but degrades at high tilts as the effective crystal thickness increases30, compounding multiple-scattering and absorption effects. This inherent tilt-dependent resolution decay is a major source of anisotropy in data from plate- or needle-like crystals11.

To obtain a high-quality dataset, we merged data from 58 individual nanocrystals using a serial MicroED strategy (“Methods”: MicroED Data Collection). In practice, we treated data collection as a serial process in which many crystals were queued for low-fluence wedges and subsequently curated and merged, rather than prospectively optimizing the minimal number of crystals required for structure solution. To maximize data completeness and mitigate the missing data wedge effect inherent to single-crystal collection, we collected a 30° or 60° data wedge from each crystal. The starting angle for each wedge was varied, ensuring that data from different crystals sampled regions of the full stage-tilt range. Even with this comprehensive collection strategy, the merged dataset exhibited the expected anisotropy. A standard spherical resolution cutoff would therefore be suboptimal, either conservatively low, discarding valuable high-resolution data, or too high, including noise from the poorly ordered directions.

To produce the most physically meaningful and high-quality dataset, we addressed anisotropy explicitly. We processed the integrated intensities with the STARANISO server33, which determines the direction-dependent resolution limits and applies a corresponding elliptical truncation. This process removes the weak, high-resolution, impaired reflections from the poorly diffracting directions while preserving the strong, high-resolution data from the well-ordered directions. Principal-axis limits and statistics are reported in Supplementary Table S2; Table 1 reports ellipsoidal statistics after truncation. Our pipeline failed at the first step for both spherical cutoffs. Using the ideal five-residue polyalanine helical fragment, PHASER did not return a valid placement for either the conservative isotropic truncation at 1.432 Å or a spherical truncation to 0.85 Å. Because no fragment placement was obtained in either case, subsequent density modification and model building could not proceed. All raw datasets and the full STARANISO output for job bzQxhc_AELS71AjMa are deposited with the raw data so that alternative truncation or scaling strategies can be tested on the same underlying measurements.

The final dataset extended to 0.85 Å (Table 1, Ellipsoidal limits) and was a critical factor in producing the high signal-to-noise ratio within this well-defined resolution ellipsoid, aided by the high multiplicity obtained through serial merging (Table 1). Observed improvements are consistent with prior reports that multiplicity improves merged MicroED data34. Analysis of the data showed no obvious evidence of specific radiation damage35. No significant difference map peaks appeared at susceptible sites such as disulfide bonds or acidic residues.

Ab initio phasing and automated structure completion

A central achievement of this work was solving the structure without a homologous model. Our workflow, conceptually similar to the fragment-based Fragon36 pipeline developed for X-ray data, began with molecular replacement in PHASER37 using a generic five-residue polyalanine helix. This yielded a low-scoring solution (TFZ=7.1) with a non-interpretable potential map (Fig. 2A, Supplementary Video 1); however, these initial phases were sufficient to bootstrap the dynamic density modification algorithm in ACORN38. This fragment-based phasing approach is similar to the strategies recently used to solve the structures of lysozyme and Proteinase K by MicroED20, similar to the ARCIMBOLDO39 and SHELXE40 based workflows. This approach resolved the phase ambiguity and produced an interpretable map covering the chain (Fig. 2B, Supplementary Video 2). The density-modified map was sufficient for BUCCANEER41 to automatically build 100% of the crambin model in a single pass. The final structure was refined with the applied twin model and ellipsoidal truncation to Rwork/Rfree values of 15.54% / 16.41%, yielding a model with excellent stereochemistry (Table 1). While these values are higher than typical X-ray structures at this resolution, they are characteristic of MicroED refinements where dynamical scattering effects are not fully modeled by standard kinematic refinement20. A hydrogen- and disorder-refined model is provided in the Supplementary Information (Supplementary Files); these coordinates are not used for Table 1 statistics. The maps from REFMAC resolve all non-hydrogen atoms and many hydrogen atoms, consistent with atomic resolution (Fig. 1F, Supplementary Fig. S5).

Positioning crambin among ab initio MicroED benchmarks

We compare this result with prior ab initio MicroED structures of triclinic lysozyme and proteinase K in Supplementary Table S4, summarizing resolution, completeness, R values, phasing fragments, microscope voltage, detector mode, and FIB use. Crambin complements these benchmarks as a sub-ångström, 200 kV, no-FIB, no energy-filter case with natural isoform heterogeneity. Representative overlays of electron potential, X-ray electron density, and neutron scattering-length maps are shown in Supplementary Fig. S5, highlighting complementary features. Crambin thus provides a useful reference point across modalities for electron-specific method development.

Crystal habit and implications for MicroED

The inversion of crystal quality, where X-ray-ideal blocks failed in MicroED while X-ray-unsuitable needles excelled, is rooted in the physical limitations of electron diffraction. The primary determinant for high-quality MicroED data is crystal thickness along the beam path, ideally below twice the inelastic mean free path (about 500–600 nm)30, to minimize dynamical scattering and absorption. While the block-like crystals possessed high internal order for X-rays, mechanically crushing them did not reliably produce fragments this thin; most remained too thick, degrading the electron diffraction. The spontaneously formed needles, however, were inherently thin in one dimension. When lying flat on the grid, they presented an ideal, electron-transparent path for the beam. This favorable habit introduces a severe preferred orientation. We directly overcame this challenge by using a serial crystallography approach, merging data from 58 crystals to build the necessary completeness.

Complementary chemical information in electron potential maps

Electron potential maps differ from X-ray electron-density and neutron scattering length density maps and can be sensitive to charge; hydrogen visibility is illustrated in Supplementary Fig. S549–52. We anticipate use of these data and maps for modeling electron scattering, hydrogen visualization, and charge-density analysis in future studies. This high-quality electron-based model, when combined with existing ultra-high-resolution X-ray and neutron data, including the 0.70 Å room-temperature solvent structure of crambin, creates an opportunity for joint and cross-modality refinement that can probe hydrogen bonding, protonation, and dynamic solvent organization in a single benchmark system26.

We determined the 0.85 Å ab initio MicroED structure of crambin directly from spontaneously formed nanocrystals obtained during ethanolic extraction. Data were collected at 200 kV without focused-ion-beam milling or an energy filter, and serial merging mitigated preferred orientation. Ellipsoidal truncation addressed anisotropy (Table 1; Supplementary Table S2). Using a minimal five-residue helical fragment and density modification, we obtained phases and automatically built the complete model (Fig. 2). Mixed PL/SI isoforms at residues 22 and 25 were refined as alternates with occupancies summing to 1, supported by omit-map evidence and an additional X-ray structure (Supplementary Files). Key statistics are reported in Table 1.
paper_content.methods:
Protein isolation and nanocrystal formation

Crambin was extracted from 230 g of manually de-husked and then crushed Crambe abyssinica seeds following a modified protocol53,54. The ground kernels were first defatted with hexane and then subjected to three rounds of extraction with 80% acetone in water (% v/v). After evaporation of the acetone under reduced pressure, the aqueous solution was stored at 4 °C for 18 h. This solution yielded a pale-yellow solid pellet upon centrifugation, which was redissolved in a 70% ethanol-water mixture (% v/v). During routine inspection, a 1 µL droplet of the ethanolic protein solution left to evaporate on a microscope slide rapidly nucleated a dense shower of sub-micron, needle-shaped crystals. These spontaneously formed nanocrystals were used for all MicroED experiments. The full detailed extraction protocol is available in the Supplementary Methods.

MicroED grid preparation and data collection

Holey-carbon copper grids (Quantifoil Cu300 R1.2/1.3) or lacey carbon grids (Cu200, Electron Microscopy Sciences) were glow-discharged (15 mA, 30 s). The grids were transferred to either a Leica GP2 plunge freezer or Thermo-Fisher Vitrobot, equilibrated to 4 °C and 95% relative humidity. A 3 µL aliquot of the crystalline slurry was applied, blotted for approximately 30 s, and plunge-frozen in liquid ethane. MicroED data were recorded on a Glacios TEM (200 kV, λ = 0.0251 Å) equipped with a Falcon 4 detector. Two sets of data were collected using SerialEM55,56: linear-mode datasets (0.2° per frame; 1.6 e− Å−2 total exposure) and counting-mode datasets (0.1° per frame; 0.8 e− Å−2 total exposure). Approximate absorbed dose estimates (MGy) for these datasets are given in Supplementary Table S4. This combination was used to capture robust low-resolution intensities (linear) and accurate high-resolution intensities (counting). This dual-mode strategy was designed to mitigate potential coincidence loss (CL) for intense low-resolution reflections, a known challenge for counting detectors in diffraction46. The total exposure per crystal that was used for MicroED data collection was kept below 2 e− Å−2. In both schemes, the starting angle of each wedge was incremented stepwise so that the combined datasets sample a stage tilt range of ±60°. Counting-mode and linear-mode datasets were collected on different crystals. We acquired 39 linear-mode datasets and used 30 of them in the final merged structure, and we acquired 117 counting-mode datasets and used 28 of them, after removing low-quality and non-merging datasets. While a lower number of crystals might be sufficient in an ideal case, the high redundancy from 58 crystals was critical for mitigating preferred orientation and achieving high signal-to-noise34. In practice, data collection followed a serial MicroED strategy analogous to single-particle workflows, where many crystals were queued for collection and subsequently curated and merged, rather than prospectively optimizing the minimal number of crystals required for structure solution. The low-flux conditions used here (~0.01–0.03 e−/Å²/s) are in a regime where CL has recently been confirmed to be present, albeit minimal, and can manifest as pseudo-twinning46. Our cautious approach was validated by this recent work, and the high quality of our merged dataset suggests the impact of CL was not severe in this case. A detailed summary of the datasets used for merging is provided in Supplementary Table S5.

Data processing and refinement

Raw movie frames were converted to the miniCBF format using a custom Python pipeline that performed 2×2 binning and a two-pass, smoothed beam-center correction (see Supplementary Methods for full details). The corrected images were processed with XDS (BUILD 20230630) and scaled with XSCALE. Datasets were curated with XSCALE_ISOCLUSTER prior to merging. The final merged dataset from 58 crystals was processed by the STARANISO server for direction-dependent resolution analysis and ellipsoidal truncation. Principal-axis limits and per-axis statistics are listed in Supplementary Table S2; ellipsoidal statistics are reported in Table 1. Phasing was performed using a combination of Phaser and ACORN, followed by automated model building in BUCCANEER. The final structure was refined using REFMAC5 with explicit modeling of a twin fraction. This twinning is consistent with pseudo-merohedry, though we note that coincidence loss in counting-detector data can also be registered as pseudo-twinning46. Isoform heterogeneity at residues 22 and 25 was modeled with alternate residue types (PL and SI) with occupancies constrained to sum to 1 using SHELXL. Final data collection and refinement statistics are provided in Table 1; Supplementary Table S6. Full .ins/.res/.fcf SHELX files are provided for both the X-ray and MicroED structures in Supplementary File 1 (hydrogen/disorder refinement).

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Protein atomic structure is crucial across various disciplines, including microbiology, biochemistry, and pharmacy. The challenges in such research lie in the high requirements for spatial resolution and the extremely complex dynamics of proteins. This manuscript reports an important research outcome, demonstrating the potential of MicroED technology in resolving atomic-resolution protein structures. The research methods used in the article are both novel and rigorous. The manuscript is well-written and filled with passion. I would recommend the publication of this significant work in Nature Communications without hesitation, provided the following issues are addressed:
Major Issues:
1. The manuscript focuses on the spontaneous formation of nanocrystals during ethanolic extraction. Have the authors explored the possibility of controlling the crystal size and morphology by varying extraction conditions (e.g., solvent type, concentration, temperature)? Such information could be valuable for optimizing MicroED experiments with other proteins. Why is needle-shaped crystal preferred compared with the block-like crystals?
2. It is surprising to me that the crushed fragments of the bulk crystal could not preserve the internal atomic order. From Fig. S3c, I noticed that the crushed fragments still maintain a relatively large size (~100 μm), which should, in principle, preserve the structural information of the crystal.
3. The authors should cite previous works regarding the crystallographic information of the crystal and compare them with the current study. I noticed that the reported lattice parameters in the following reference differ from those in this work. The authors should explain this discrepancy: (Ref. 42: Solvent organization in the ultrahigh-resolution crystal structure of crambin at room temperature, https://doi.org/10.1107/S2052252524007784)
4. The crambin protein exists in two natural isomers, PL and SI, and a hybrid model with partial occupancies was successfully built. Did the authors perform further analysis and comparison of the structures and relationships of these two isomers?
Minor Issues:
1. Page 2, “Crystals invisible to the naked eye,”: Missing “are.”
2. A citation should be added for this information: "It was later the first protein solved by Hauptman and Weeks’ purely mathematical direct methods, a triumph developed at our home institutions."
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This study presents the first ab initio structure of crambin solved by MicroED, achieving the highest reported data quality to date in terms of resolution, completeness, and R values. As the authors note, this work establishes an important gold-standard reference for the future development of electron crystallography, including modelling electron scattering, analyzing charge density, and exploring hydrogen-bonding networks. The manuscript would be further strengthened by addressing the following points prior to publication.
1. The authors repeatedly state that ‘Our workflow demonstrates that complex biological matrices can be mined directly for sub-ångström protein structures, establishing a practical and scalable pipeline from raw biomass to atomic-level models of previously intractable targets’. While this claim is compelling, a discussion is needed regarding the general applicability of this pipeline. Specifically, how broadly can high-resolution MicroED data be obtained directly from seeds for ab initio structure determination? For instance, is the proposed “low-tech” crystallization method generally effective for all small proteins? How frequently do crystals of suitable size and sufficient crystallinity arise for MicroED experiments using this approach? The authors should comment on these practical aspects to clarify the scope and limitations of their workflow.
2. You note that previous ab initio structures have been obtained by MicroED for triclinic lysozyme and proteinase K (for example, see Nature Methods, DOI:10.1038/s41592-022-01485-4). It would be valuable for the authors to address how their crambin structure compares to these earlier achievements. Specifically:
Why might crambin serve as a more suitable gold-standard reference for advancing electron-specific methods?
Is the choice driven primarily by superior data quality—such as finer resolution, improved completeness, better R values, or enhanced signal-to-noise?
Could the data quality for triclinic lysozyme and proteinase K be further enhanced, and if not, what limitations prevent further improvement?
A discussion along these lines would clarify the rationale for highlighting crambin and help frame its broader significance in the field.
3. On lines 23–29, the authors state that “the crushed fragments produced markedly inferior electron diffraction data compared to the spontaneously formed needles.” This finding contrasts with the results reported by M. Jason de la Cruz and colleagues (Nat Methods, DOI:10.1038/nmeth.4178), who found that crushed crystals could yield high-quality diffraction.
Could the authors elaborate on why this difference arises in the case of crambin? A comparison of methodological details and crystal behavior between crambin and other proteins would clarify why the crushed-fragment approach performed differently here and provide valuable insight into the limits of this technique.
4. The authors applied anisotropy correction to the data using STARANISO, reporting an effective (ellipsoidal) completeness of 98.6%. It would be valuable to also provide the data statistics along the two principal axes of the ellipsoid for clarity. In addition, could the authors comment on whether ab initio structure determination would still be feasible without applying anisotropy correction, and if so, how large the differences in outcome (e.g., resolution limits, map interpretability, or refinement statistics) would be?
5. A minor comment regarding Fig. 1E: it is not immediately clear that the highest observed reflection extends to 0.85 Å. The authors should highlight this more explicitly in the figure to aid clarity.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Vasireddy et al. report on a method to solve the structure of proteins without a homologous model. In this opportunity, they used the spontaneously formed microcrystals of the seed protein crambin, avoiding the preparation of large size crystals for X-ray or the time-consuming FIB lamella preparation for MicroED. The ultra-high resolution (0.85Å) microED data allowed structure resolution using a five-alanine helical fragment to initiate density modification.
General comments:
The novelty of the report relies on being the first ab initio structure of the protein crambin determined by electron-diffraction. While validation of existing methods is valuable, the study does not introduce significant novelty or advance the field beyond confirming the applicability of ab initio phasing using minimal idealized fragments followed by density modification improvement [Martynowycz et al. Nature Methods 19, 724–729 (2022)]. The study's contribution to the field is incremental. It provides confirmatory evidence but does not present a major advance or novel insights.
Major Comments:
1. Authors performed serial microED to try to reduce anisotropy. They collected on 58 crystals, each one with 30° or 60° wedge. The starting angle of each wedge was incremented stepwise so that the combined datasets sample a stage tilt range of +/- 60Å. Regarding this collection strategy:
• 58 crystals could seem a large number of crystals, especially considering that the resulting merged data still displayed significant anisotropy. Assuming each crystal with at least 30° wedge, the stepwise increment between each crystal was ~2°, increasing the redundancy. I would like to see a discussion about the minimal number of crystals that would produce similar results.
• Authors reported a combination of collection in linear and counting mode. What percentage of crystals were in linear mode? Previously, Martynowycz et al. collected only on counting mode with very low exposure rate. In the present report, authors combined linear and counting modes in “the hopes the low-resolution reflections in linear mode would be less prone to coincidence loss, and the high-resolution reflections in counting mode would be more accurately recorded”. What was the effect of using linear mode collection? How did data behaved if only counting mode datasets were used? What would be the recommended strategy for future projects, counting mode only or a combination of both?
2. This report uses 0.85Å resolution data to performs molecular replacement in PHASER using a generic five-residue poly-alanine helix, and the resulting initial phases were sufficient to bootstrap the dynamic density modification algorithm in ACORN. Crambin is a protein of ~4.7kDa and 46 amino acids. While impressive, previously, Martynowycz et al. used data to 0.87Å (for lysozyme nanocrystals) and solved the structure with the same approach using a three poly-alanine fragment in PHASER followed by ACORN. The authors of the present report need to demonstrate what is novel about this work beyond what has already been published.
3. Authors claim their map provides a complementary chemical picture of crambin to those available through X-ray or neutron techniques, highlighting that crambin is benchmark protein across crystallographic platforms. However, they did not show any comparison (figures) of those structures or the difference in the information obtained on the first structure of crambin solved by electrons.
4. The statement at the end of the abstract ... “complex biological matrices can be mined directly for sub-ångström protein structures, establishing a practical and scalable pipeline from raw biomass to atomic-level models of previously intractable targets” it is an overstatement. It is very unlikely that will happen in general for other samples; unless the authors can prove otherwise.
5. Comparisons with the 0.48 Å resolution structure would be important to show including overall structure, key residues.
6. The authors should create difference maps where residues for the PI and SL isoforms are omitted from the calculation and show the map of the two possible conformations.
7. To solve a structure by ab-initio methods the required resolution needs to be higher than 1.1 Å. This corresponds to less than 1% of all protein structures solved. Hence, it would be hard to sell it as a general method.
Minor Comments:
1. In Page 2, Line 31, authors wrote:
“In subsequent years, synchrotron and neutron[23] sources pushed its resolution to an extraordinary 0.48 and 0.54 Å,[24,25] making it a key model for studying ultra-high-resolution features.”
Ref 23 reports neutron diffraction of crambin at 1.1Å. Both structures 0.48 (Ref 24) and 0.54 (Ref 25) are from X-Ray diffraction. Please rephrase the sentence to avoid confusion.
2. The conclusion section seems largely as part of the discussion. Consider moving part of this section to the discussion section and focus on delivering a strong, shorter conclusion.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
We thank the reviewers and editor for their careful evaluations of our manuscript and their constructive feedback. We are pleased they found the work significant. We have addressed all points raised, which we believe has substantially strengthened the paper.
We note that during the revision, while addressing reviewer comments on anisotropy (R2.4), we identified an input error in our original STARANISO processing that resulted in the output statistics being reported to 0.858 Å resolution but having reflections out to 0.850 Å resolution which the final structure was refined to. This was confusing. We re-processed the entire dataset from scratch, which resulted in a model and statistics table that both extend to 0.850 Å resolutions that are essentially identical to the previous model. The conclusions remain unchanged, but all tables, figures, and statistics in the revised manuscript have been updated to reflect this.
We have also added three new Supplementary Tables (S2, S3, S4) and two new Supplementary Figures (S5, S6) to directly address the reviewers' points. All changes in the manuscript are marked with tracked changes with new or revised text also highlighted.
Below, we provide a point-by-point response to each comment.
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
Protein atomic structure is crucial across various disciplines, including microbiology, biochemistry, and pharmacy. The challenges in such research lie in the high requirements for spatial resolution and the extremely complex dynamics of proteins. This manuscript reports an important research outcome, demonstrating the potential of MicroED technology in resolving atomic-resolution protein structures. The research methods used in the article are both novel and rigorous. The manuscript is well-written and filled with passion. I would recommend the publication of this significant work in Nature Communications without hesitation, provided the following issues are addressed:
RESPONSE: We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful assessment and for recommending publication. We address each point below and have made the indicated revisions.
Major Issues:
1. The manuscript focuses on the spontaneous formation of nanocrystals during ethanolic extraction. Have the authors explored the possibility of controlling the crystal size and morphology by varying extraction conditions (e.g., solvent type, concentration, temperature)? Such information could be valuable for optimizing MicroED experiments with other proteins. Why is needle-shaped crystal preferred compared with the block-like crystals?
RESPONSE: We did not systematically optimize the crystallization, as the spontaneously formed needles were already ideal for MicroED. We have added a new paragraph to the Discussion ("Crystal habit and implications for MicroED") that addresses this. It lists the variables that could plausibly tune habit (solvent, temperature, etc.) and explains precisely why needles are advantageous for MicroED (reduced effective thickness, lower dynamical scattering) and how serial merging mitigates the trade-off of preferred orientation.
2. It is surprising to me that the crushed fragments of the bulk crystal could not preserve the internal atomic order. From Fig. S3c, I noticed that the crushed fragments still maintain a relatively large size (~100 μm), which should, in principle, preserve the structural information of the crystal.
RESPONSE: This is an excellent point. We have clarified in the Results section that for electrons, the limiting factor is thickness along the beam, not lateral size. We explain that while the fragments were large laterally, most remained thicker than the ~0.5 μm useful limit, which degrades data quality via dynamical scattering. This is why the spontaneously formed, thin needles performed better. We also contrast this system-specific outcome with other reports where crushing was successful.

I noticed that the reported lattice parameters in the following reference differ from those in this work. The authors should explain this discrepancy: (Ref. 42: Solvent organization in the ultrahigh-resolution crystal structure of crambin at room temperature, https://doi.org/10.1107/S2052252524007784)
RESPONSE: We have added Supplementary Table S2 ("Crambin unit cell comparisons"). RESPONSE: Corrected.
8) Regarding the number of datasets that made the final cut to the merged data, 30 out of 39 in linear mode, and 28 out of 117 in counting mode, any reason/explanation why counting mode seems to be less favored? A full, systematic comparison of “counting only” versus “counting plus linear” merges across alternative clustering thresholds and scaling choices would substantially expand the scope of the manuscript beyond demonstrating an ab initio solution from the highest-quality merged dataset. You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

While purifying the seed protein crambin, we find that needles of pure protein nanocrystals form spontaneously during the drying of a simple ethanolic purification drop. These needles diffract X-rays weakly but are well-suited for microcrystal electron diffraction (MicroED). Merging data from 58 such nanocrystals yields diffraction to 0.85 Å resolution and solves the structure ab initio using a five-residue helical fragment to initiate density modification. The resulting map enables automated model building and resolves individual hydrogen atoms. This work reports an atomic resolution MicroED structure of the protein crambin solved ab initio. This study establishes a publicly available benchmark showing that sub-ångström ab initio MicroED can be achieved on standard 200 kV instrumentation without energy filtering or FIB milling, when serial merging is combined with anisotropy aware truncation to address preferred orientation. For this dataset, isotropic truncation alone did not produce a fragment placement suitable for phasing in this workflow, whereas applying anisotropy correction supported an ab initio solution.

---

## Introduction

Crystallography, a cornerstone method for determining protein structures, has traditionally been limited by crystal size. X-ray crystallography, the gold standard for determining atomic resolution structures, requires relatively large, well-ordered crystals - typically tens to hundreds of micrometers across. Yet many proteins naturally form only extremely tiny crystals, far smaller than this threshold, leaving a significant fraction of important biological molecules structurally inaccessible. Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), another powerful approach, struggles to achieve high-resolution structures of proteins less than 100 kDa1. This limits its utility for many biologically important molecules, e.g., the median size of a human protein is only about 40 kDa2.

Microcrystal electron diffraction (MicroED) has emerged as an approach to overcome these limitations3. Instead of X-rays, MicroED uses electrons, which interact far more strongly with matter4. This interaction allows high-resolution structure determination from crystals thousands of times smaller by volume than those required for traditional X-ray methods. Although many crystals are invisible to the naked eye5 and often too small or delicate for standard crystallography, they can still yield atomic-resolution structures using MicroED. In favorable cases, direct analysis of nanocrystalline material is possible6,7.

Despite its promise, phasing protein structures by MicroED remains heavily reliant on pre-existing knowledge. Molecular replacement (MR) for MicroED, demonstrated with lysozyme in 2013–20148,9, is the workhorse method and has delivered important structures like Ca2+-ATPase10, R2lox11, MyD8812, and the human lens membrane protein MP2013. The arrival of AlphaFold214 has further expanded the reach of MR. However, this reliance on homologous models creates a fundamental limitation: it generates phase bias and leaves proteins with novel folds inaccessible. Establishing reliable ab initio phasing methods that remove this dependence is essential. While this has been routine for small-molecule electron crystallography for years6,15–17, progress for proteins has been incremental, moving from direct methods on small peptides18, to fragment-based searches19, and recently to density-modification-based bootstrapping from minimal ideal fragments20. Prior ab initio MicroED demonstrations established feasibility, and many implementations have operated in regimes that mitigate geometric incompleteness and anisotropy, for example, by reducing thickness or by using microscope and detector configurations that broaden the usable data range. Here, we ask whether an ab initio solution remains achievable on widely available 200 kV hardware without energy filtration or FIB milling, and we assess whether anisotropy-aware data treatment is a practical determinant of success in this dataset, a consideration that may be important in similarly anisotropic cases. Rather than introducing a new phasing algorithm, our goal is to provide a well-characterized, publicly available atomic resolution MicroED benchmark that complements existing lysozyme and proteinase K datasets and enables rigorous testing of electron-specific methods.

In this study, we bridge this methodological gap by using the classic benchmark protein crambin21. For decades, Crambin has served as a proving ground for the most advanced crystallographic methods. Its 1981 structure by Hendrickson and Teeter was a landmark in de novo phasing using sulfur anomalous scattering22, and it was later the protein solved by Hauptman and Weeks’ purely mathematical direct methods, a triumph developed at our home institutions23. Subsequent X-ray studies reached 0.48 Å24 and 0.54 Å25, and more recently, a 0.70 Å26 room-temperature X-ray structure provided an ultrahigh-resolution description of the crambin solvent network and disorder in the PL and SI isoforms. Furthermore, neutron diffraction has been reported to 1.1 Å resolution at room temperature27.

Despite this storied history in X-ray and neutron science, a completed de novo investigation of crambin by MicroED has remained unexplored. While a 1.07 Å MicroED structure solved by molecular replacement has been briefly described in a technical note (Rigaku Application note PX031)28, the full potential of using electrons to solve this benchmark protein from first principles has not been realized. We discovered that a simple ethanolic extraction from finely ground seeds spontaneously yields an abundant supply of nanocrystals ideal for such a test. Therefore, we set an ambitious goal: to determine if data from these naturally formed nanocrystals were of sufficient quality to not only break the sub-ångström barrier but to solve the structure ab initio from a minimal, non-homologous five-residue helical fragment29.

Here we report an electron ab initio structure of crambin at sub-ångström resolution obtained directly from spontaneously formed nanocrystals collected on standard 200 kV hardware without using a focused ion-beam to thin the crystals or an energy filter, with data merged from multiple crystals to mitigate preferred orientation. We position crambin as a reference for electron-specific methods and compare it with prior ab initio MicroED results.

---

## Results

At a tale of two crystals: swapping fortunes in X-ray and electron diffraction

Our investigation began with a serendipitous discovery. During a simple ethanolic extraction of crushed Crambe abyssinica seeds (Supplementary Fig. S1), we found that a 1 µL droplet of the protein-rich solution nucleated a dense shower of sub-micron, needle-shaped crystals within seconds as the solvent evaporated (Fig. 1A). These crystals formed without a separate screening step. These needles proved unsuitable for X-ray diffraction. A single 14 µm needle diffracted poorly, only reaching 1.6 Å resolution and suffered from rapid radiation decay (Supplementary Fig. S2, Supplementary Table S1). In contrast, they proved ideal for MicroED. When loaded into the TEM, we noticed many tiny rod-shaped crystals on the grid (Fig. 1B). High-resolution imaging of these crystals showed clear lattice lines (Fig. 1C) that contained information to 3.6 Å by analysis of the Fourier transform of these images (Fig. 1D). These crystals consistently diffracted electrons to high resolution (Fig. 1E).

We also grew large, block-like crystals using traditional vapor diffusion (Supplementary Fig. S3). These crystals exhibited the opposite behavior: they produced excellent X-ray diffraction to beyond 0.8 Å but were too thick for MicroED. We mechanically crushed these blocks to obtain fragments for MicroED, but the crushed fragments produced markedly inferior electron diffraction data compared to the spontaneously formed needles (Supplementary Fig. S4). For electrons, the limiting dimension is thickness along the beam (below twice the inelastic mean free path, or about 500 to 600 nm)30; most crushed fragments remained too thick, increasing dynamical scattering and absorption. This system-specific outcome contrasts with reports where crushed fragments diffracted well, such as De La Cruz et al.31, where fragmentation produced abundant electron-transparent crystals; here the spontaneous needles provided higher-quality MicroED data.

This inversion of crystal quality between the two diffraction methods motivated our collection strategy. Rather than rely on non-ideal fragments to randomize orientation, we tackled the preferred orientation problem of the spontaneously formed needles directly using a serial crystallography approach. By merging data from multiple crystals, we aimed to overcome geometric data loss inherent to a single orientation and build a complete, high-redundancy dataset.

Achieving an atomic-resolution microED dataset by overcoming anisotropy

Having established the superiority of the spontaneously formed nanocrystals for MicroED experiments, we proceeded with data collection. The primary technical hurdle was, as anticipated, the severe preferred orientation of the needles on the grid32. This morphology introduces a fundamental challenge for MicroED: diffraction quality is highest at low tilt angles, where the electron beam passes through the thinnest dimension of the crystal, but degrades at high tilts as the effective crystal thickness increases30, compounding multiple-scattering and absorption effects. This inherent tilt-dependent resolution decay is a major source of anisotropy in data from plate- or needle-like crystals11.

To obtain a high-quality dataset, we merged data from 58 individual nanocrystals using a serial MicroED strategy (“Methods”: MicroED Data Collection). In practice, we treated data collection as a serial process in which many crystals were queued for low-fluence wedges and subsequently curated and merged, rather than prospectively optimizing the minimal number of crystals required for structure solution. To maximize data completeness and mitigate the missing data wedge effect inherent to single-crystal collection, we collected a 30° or 60° data wedge from each crystal. The starting angle for each wedge was varied, ensuring that data from different crystals sampled regions of the full stage-tilt range. Even with this comprehensive collection strategy, the merged dataset exhibited the expected anisotropy. A standard spherical resolution cutoff would therefore be suboptimal, either conservatively low, discarding valuable high-resolution data, or too high, including noise from the poorly ordered directions.

To produce the most physically meaningful and high-quality dataset, we addressed anisotropy explicitly. We processed the integrated intensities with the STARANISO server33, which determines the direction-dependent resolution limits and applies a corresponding elliptical truncation. This process removes the weak, high-resolution, impaired reflections from the poorly diffracting directions while preserving the strong, high-resolution data from the well-ordered directions. Principal-axis limits and statistics are reported in Supplementary Table S2; Table 1 reports ellipsoidal statistics after truncation. Our pipeline failed at the first step for both spherical cutoffs. Using the ideal five-residue polyalanine helical fragment, PHASER did not return a valid placement for either the conservative isotropic truncation at 1.432 Å or a spherical truncation to 0.85 Å. Because no fragment placement was obtained in either case, subsequent density modification and model building could not proceed. All raw datasets and the full STARANISO output for job bzQxhc_AELS71AjMa are deposited with the raw data so that alternative truncation or scaling strategies can be tested on the same underlying measurements.

The final dataset extended to 0.85 Å (Table 1, Ellipsoidal limits) and was a critical factor in producing the high signal-to-noise ratio within this well-defined resolution ellipsoid, aided by the high multiplicity obtained through serial merging (Table 1). Observed improvements are consistent with prior reports that multiplicity improves merged MicroED data34. Analysis of the data showed no obvious evidence of specific radiation damage35. No significant difference map peaks appeared at susceptible sites such as disulfide bonds or acidic residues.

Ab initio phasing and automated structure completion

A central achievement of this work was solving the structure without a homologous model. Our workflow, conceptually similar to the fragment-based Fragon36 pipeline developed for X-ray data, began with molecular replacement in PHASER37 using a generic five-residue polyalanine helix. This yielded a low-scoring solution (TFZ=7.1) with a non-interpretable potential map (Fig. 2A, Supplementary Video 1); however, these initial phases were sufficient to bootstrap the dynamic density modification algorithm in ACORN38. This fragment-based phasing approach is similar to the strategies recently used to solve the structures of lysozyme and Proteinase K by MicroED20, similar to the ARCIMBOLDO39 and SHELXE40 based workflows. This approach resolved the phase ambiguity and produced an interpretable map covering the chain (Fig. 2B, Supplementary Video 2). The density-modified map was sufficient for BUCCANEER41 to automatically build 100% of the crambin model in a single pass. The final structure was refined with the applied twin model and ellipsoidal truncation to Rwork/Rfree values of 15.54% / 16.41%, yielding a model with excellent stereochemistry (Table 1). While these values are higher than typical X-ray structures at this resolution, they are characteristic of MicroED refinements where dynamical scattering effects are not fully modeled by standard kinematic refinement20. A hydrogen- and disorder-refined model is provided in the Supplementary Information (Supplementary Files); these coordinates are not used for Table 1 statistics. The maps from REFMAC resolve all non-hydrogen atoms and many hydrogen atoms, consistent with atomic resolution (Fig. 1F, Supplementary Fig. S5).

Positioning crambin among ab initio MicroED benchmarks

We compare this result with prior ab initio MicroED structures of triclinic lysozyme and proteinase K in Supplementary Table S4, summarizing resolution, completeness, R values, phasing fragments, microscope voltage, detector mode, and FIB use. Crambin complements these benchmarks as a sub-ångström, 200 kV, no-FIB, no energy-filter case with natural isoform heterogeneity. Representative overlays of electron potential, X-ray electron density, and neutron scattering-length maps are shown in Supplementary Fig. S5, highlighting complementary features. Crambin thus provides a useful reference point across modalities for electron-specific method development.

Crystal habit and implications for MicroED

The inversion of crystal quality, where X-ray-ideal blocks failed in MicroED while X-ray-unsuitable needles excelled, is rooted in the physical limitations of electron diffraction. The primary determinant for high-quality MicroED data is crystal thickness along the beam path, ideally below twice the inelastic mean free path (about 500–600 nm)30, to minimize dynamical scattering and absorption. While the block-like crystals possessed high internal order for X-rays, mechanically crushing them did not reliably produce fragments this thin; most remained too thick, degrading the electron diffraction. The spontaneously formed needles, however, were inherently thin in one dimension. When lying flat on the grid, they presented an ideal, electron-transparent path for the beam. This favorable habit introduces a severe preferred orientation. We directly overcame this challenge by using a serial crystallography approach, merging data from 58 crystals to build the necessary completeness.

Complementary chemical information in electron potential maps

Electron potential maps differ from X-ray electron-density and neutron scattering length density maps and can be sensitive to charge; hydrogen visibility is illustrated in Supplementary Fig. S549–52. We anticipate use of these data and maps for modeling electron scattering, hydrogen visualization, and charge-density analysis in future studies. This high-quality electron-based model, when combined with existing ultra-high-resolution X-ray and neutron data, including the 0.70 Å room-temperature solvent structure of crambin, creates an opportunity for joint and cross-modality refinement that can probe hydrogen bonding, protonation, and dynamic solvent organization in a single benchmark system26.

We determined the 0.85 Å ab initio MicroED structure of crambin directly from spontaneously formed nanocrystals obtained during ethanolic extraction. Data were collected at 200 kV without focused-ion-beam milling or an energy filter, and serial merging mitigated preferred orientation. Ellipsoidal truncation addressed anisotropy (Table 1; Supplementary Table S2). Using a minimal five-residue helical fragment and density modification, we obtained phases and automatically built the complete model (Fig. 2). Mixed PL/SI isoforms at residues 22 and 25 were refined as alternates with occupancies summing to 1, supported by omit-map evidence and an additional X-ray structure (Supplementary Files). Key statistics are reported in Table 1.

---

## Methods

Protein isolation and nanocrystal formation

Crambin was extracted from 230 g of manually de-husked and then crushed Crambe abyssinica seeds following a modified protocol53,54. The ground kernels were first defatted with hexane and then subjected to three rounds of extraction with 80% acetone in water (% v/v). After evaporation of the acetone under reduced pressure, the aqueous solution was stored at 4 °C for 18 h. This solution yielded a pale-yellow solid pellet upon centrifugation, which was redissolved in a 70% ethanol-water mixture (% v/v). During routine inspection, a 1 µL droplet of the ethanolic protein solution left to evaporate on a microscope slide rapidly nucleated a dense shower of sub-micron, needle-shaped crystals. These spontaneously formed nanocrystals were used for all MicroED experiments. The full detailed extraction protocol is available in the Supplementary Methods.

MicroED grid preparation and data collection

Holey-carbon copper grids (Quantifoil Cu300 R1.2/1.3) or lacey carbon grids (Cu200, Electron Microscopy Sciences) were glow-discharged (15 mA, 30 s). The grids were transferred to either a Leica GP2 plunge freezer or Thermo-Fisher Vitrobot, equilibrated to 4 °C and 95% relative humidity. A 3 µL aliquot of the crystalline slurry was applied, blotted for approximately 30 s, and plunge-frozen in liquid ethane. MicroED data were recorded on a Glacios TEM (200 kV, λ = 0.0251 Å) equipped with a Falcon 4 detector. Two sets of data were collected using SerialEM55,56: linear-mode datasets (0.2° per frame; 1.6 e− Å−2 total exposure) and counting-mode datasets (0.1° per frame; 0.8 e− Å−2 total exposure). Approximate absorbed dose estimates (MGy) for these datasets are given in Supplementary Table S4. This combination was used to capture robust low-resolution intensities (linear) and accurate high-resolution intensities (counting). This dual-mode strategy was designed to mitigate potential coincidence loss (CL) for intense low-resolution reflections, a known challenge for counting detectors in diffraction46. The total exposure per crystal that was used for MicroED data collection was kept below 2 e− Å−2. In both schemes, the starting angle of each wedge was incremented stepwise so that the combined datasets sample a stage tilt range of ±60°. Counting-mode and linear-mode datasets were collected on different crystals. We acquired 39 linear-mode datasets and used 30 of them in the final merged structure, and we acquired 117 counting-mode datasets and used 28 of them, after removing low-quality and non-merging datasets. While a lower number of crystals might be sufficient in an ideal case, the high redundancy from 58 crystals was critical for mitigating preferred orientation and achieving high signal-to-noise34. In practice, data collection followed a serial MicroED strategy analogous to single-particle workflows, where many crystals were queued for collection and subsequently curated and merged, rather than prospectively optimizing the minimal number of crystals required for structure solution. The low-flux conditions used here (~0.01–0.03 e−/Å²/s) are in a regime where CL has recently been confirmed to be present, albeit minimal, and can manifest as pseudo-twinning46. Our cautious approach was validated by this recent work, and the high quality of our merged dataset suggests the impact of CL was not severe in this case. A detailed summary of the datasets used for merging is provided in Supplementary Table S5.

Data processing and refinement

Raw movie frames were converted to the miniCBF format using a custom Python pipeline that performed 2×2 binning and a two-pass, smoothed beam-center correction (see Supplementary Methods for full details). The corrected images were processed with XDS (BUILD 20230630) and scaled with XSCALE. Datasets were curated with XSCALE_ISOCLUSTER prior to merging. The final merged dataset from 58 crystals was processed by the STARANISO server for direction-dependent resolution analysis and ellipsoidal truncation. Principal-axis limits and per-axis statistics are listed in Supplementary Table S2; ellipsoidal statistics are reported in Table 1. Phasing was performed using a combination of Phaser and ACORN, followed by automated model building in BUCCANEER. The final structure was refined using REFMAC5 with explicit modeling of a twin fraction. This twinning is consistent with pseudo-merohedry, though we note that coincidence loss in counting-detector data can also be registered as pseudo-twinning46. Isoform heterogeneity at residues 22 and 25 was modeled with alternate residue types (PL and SI) with occupancies constrained to sum to 1 using SHELXL. Final data collection and refinement statistics are provided in Table 1; Supplementary Table S6. Full .ins/.res/.fcf SHELX files are provided for both the X-ray and MicroED structures in Supplementary File 1 (hydrogen/disorder refinement).

## Abstract

## Introduction

Crystallography, a cornerstone method for determining protein structures, has traditionally been limited by crystal size. X-ray crystallography, the gold standard for determining atomic resolution structures, requires relatively large, well-ordered crystals - typically tens to hundreds of micrometers across. Yet many proteins naturally form only extremely tiny crystals, far smaller than this threshold, leaving a significant fraction of important biological molecules structurally inaccessible. Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), another powerful approach, struggles to achieve high-resolution structures of proteins less than 100 kDa1. This limits its utility for many biologically important molecules, e.g., the median size of a human protein is only about 40 kDa2.

Microcrystal electron diffraction (MicroED) has emerged as an approach to overcome these limitations3. Instead of X-rays, MicroED uses electrons, which interact far more strongly with matter4. This interaction allows high-resolution structure determination from crystals thousands of times smaller by volume than those required for traditional X-ray methods. Although many crystals are invisible to the naked eye5 and often too small or delicate for standard crystallography, they can still yield atomic-resolution structures using MicroED. In favorable cases, direct analysis of nanocrystalline material is possible6,7.

Despite its promise, phasing protein structures by MicroED remains heavily reliant on pre-existing knowledge. Molecular replacement (MR) for MicroED, demonstrated with lysozyme in 2013–20148,9, is the workhorse method and has delivered important structures like Ca2+-ATPase10, R2lox11, MyD8812, and the human lens membrane protein MP2013. The arrival of AlphaFold214 has further expanded the reach of MR. However, this reliance on homologous models creates a fundamental limitation: it generates phase bias and leaves proteins with novel folds inaccessible. Establishing reliable ab initio phasing methods that remove this dependence is essential. While this has been routine for small-molecule electron crystallography for years6,15–17, progress for proteins has been incremental, moving from direct methods on small peptides18, to fragment-based searches19, and recently to density-modification-based bootstrapping from minimal ideal fragments20. Prior ab initio MicroED demonstrations established feasibility, and many implementations have operated in regimes that mitigate geometric incompleteness and anisotropy, for example, by reducing thickness or by using microscope and detector configurations that broaden the usable data range. Here, we ask whether an ab initio solution remains achievable on widely available 200 kV hardware without energy filtration or FIB milling, and we assess whether anisotropy-aware data treatment is a practical determinant of success in this dataset, a consideration that may be important in similarly anisotropic cases. Rather than introducing a new phasing algorithm, our goal is to provide a well-characterized, publicly available atomic resolution MicroED benchmark that complements existing lysozyme and proteinase K datasets and enables rigorous testing of electron-specific methods.

In this study, we bridge this methodological gap by using the classic benchmark protein crambin21. For decades, Crambin has served as a proving ground for the most advanced crystallographic methods. Its 1981 structure by Hendrickson and Teeter was a landmark in de novo phasing using sulfur anomalous scattering22, and it was later the protein solved by Hauptman and Weeks’ purely mathematical direct methods, a triumph developed at our home institutions23. Subsequent X-ray studies reached 0.48 Å24 and 0.54 Å25, and more recently, a 0.70 Å26 room-temperature X-ray structure provided an ultrahigh-resolution description of the crambin solvent network and disorder in the PL and SI isoforms. Furthermore, neutron diffraction has been reported to 1.1 Å resolution at room temperature27.

Despite this storied history in X-ray and neutron science, a completed de novo investigation of crambin by MicroED has remained unexplored. While a 1.07 Å MicroED structure solved by molecular replacement has been briefly described in a technical note (Rigaku Application note PX031)28, the full potential of using electrons to solve this benchmark protein from first principles has not been realized. We discovered that a simple ethanolic extraction from finely ground seeds spontaneously yields an abundant supply of nanocrystals ideal for such a test. Therefore, we set an ambitious goal: to determine if data from these naturally formed nanocrystals were of sufficient quality to not only break the sub-ångström barrier but to solve the structure ab initio from a minimal, non-homologous five-residue helical fragment29.

Here we report an electron ab initio structure of crambin at sub-ångström resolution obtained directly from spontaneously formed nanocrystals collected on standard 200 kV hardware without using a focused ion-beam to thin the crystals or an energy filter, with data merged from multiple crystals to mitigate preferred orientation. We position crambin as a reference for electron-specific methods and compare it with prior ab initio MicroED results.

---

## Results

At a tale of two crystals: swapping fortunes in X-ray and electron diffraction

Our investigation began with a serendipitous discovery. During a simple ethanolic extraction of crushed Crambe abyssinica seeds (Supplementary Fig. S1), we found that a 1 µL droplet of the protein-rich solution nucleated a dense shower of sub-micron, needle-shaped crystals within seconds as the solvent evaporated (Fig. 1A). These crystals formed without a separate screening step. These needles proved unsuitable for X-ray diffraction. A single 14 µm needle diffracted poorly, only reaching 1.6 Å resolution and suffered from rapid radiation decay (Supplementary Fig. S2, Supplementary Table S1). In contrast, they proved ideal for MicroED. When loaded into the TEM, we noticed many tiny rod-shaped crystals on the grid (Fig. 1B). High-resolution imaging of these crystals showed clear lattice lines (Fig. 1C) that contained information to 3.6 Å by analysis of the Fourier transform of these images (Fig. 1D). These crystals consistently diffracted electrons to high resolution (Fig. 1E).

We also grew large, block-like crystals using traditional vapor diffusion (Supplementary Fig. S3). These crystals exhibited the opposite behavior: they produced excellent X-ray diffraction to beyond 0.8 Å but were too thick for MicroED. We mechanically crushed these blocks to obtain fragments for MicroED, but the crushed fragments produced markedly inferior electron diffraction data compared to the spontaneously formed needles (Supplementary Fig. S4). For electrons, the limiting dimension is thickness along the beam (below twice the inelastic mean free path, or about 500 to 600 nm)30; most crushed fragments remained too thick, increasing dynamical scattering and absorption. This system-specific outcome contrasts with reports where crushed fragments diffracted well, such as De La Cruz et al.31, where fragmentation produced abundant electron-transparent crystals; here the spontaneous needles provided higher-quality MicroED data.

This inversion of crystal quality between the two diffraction methods motivated our collection strategy. Rather than rely on non-ideal fragments to randomize orientation, we tackled the preferred orientation problem of the spontaneously formed needles directly using a serial crystallography approach. By merging data from multiple crystals, we aimed to overcome geometric data loss inherent to a single orientation and build a complete, high-redundancy dataset.

Achieving an atomic-resolution microED dataset by overcoming anisotropy

Having established the superiority of the spontaneously formed nanocrystals for MicroED experiments, we proceeded with data collection. The primary technical hurdle was, as anticipated, the severe preferred orientation of the needles on the grid32. This morphology introduces a fundamental challenge for MicroED: diffraction quality is highest at low tilt angles, where the electron beam passes through the thinnest dimension of the crystal, but degrades at high tilts as the effective crystal thickness increases30, compounding multiple-scattering and absorption effects. This inherent tilt-dependent resolution decay is a major source of anisotropy in data from plate- or needle-like crystals11.

To obtain a high-quality dataset, we merged data from 58 individual nanocrystals using a serial MicroED strategy (“Methods”: MicroED Data Collection). In practice, we treated data collection as a serial process in which many crystals were queued for low-fluence wedges and subsequently curated and merged, rather than prospectively optimizing the minimal number of crystals required for structure solution. To maximize data completeness and mitigate the missing data wedge effect inherent to single-crystal collection, we collected a 30° or 60° data wedge from each crystal. The starting angle for each wedge was varied, ensuring that data from different crystals sampled regions of the full stage-tilt range. Even with this comprehensive collection strategy, the merged dataset exhibited the expected anisotropy. A standard spherical resolution cutoff would therefore be suboptimal, either conservatively low, discarding valuable high-resolution data, or too high, including noise from the poorly ordered directions.

To produce the most physically meaningful and high-quality dataset, we addressed anisotropy explicitly. We processed the integrated intensities with the STARANISO server33, which determines the direction-dependent resolution limits and applies a corresponding elliptical truncation. This process removes the weak, high-resolution, impaired reflections from the poorly diffracting directions while preserving the strong, high-resolution data from the well-ordered directions. Principal-axis limits and statistics are reported in Supplementary Table S2; Table 1 reports ellipsoidal statistics after truncation. Our pipeline failed at the first step for both spherical cutoffs. Using the ideal five-residue polyalanine helical fragment, PHASER did not return a valid placement for either the conservative isotropic truncation at 1.432 Å or a spherical truncation to 0.85 Å. Because no fragment placement was obtained in either case, subsequent density modification and model building could not proceed. All raw datasets and the full STARANISO output for job bzQxhc_AELS71AjMa are deposited with the raw data so that alternative truncation or scaling strategies can be tested on the same underlying measurements.

The final dataset extended to 0.85 Å (Table 1, Ellipsoidal limits) and was a critical factor in producing the high signal-to-noise ratio within this well-defined resolution ellipsoid, aided by the high multiplicity obtained through serial merging (Table 1). Observed improvements are consistent with prior reports that multiplicity improves merged MicroED data34. Analysis of the data showed no obvious evidence of specific radiation damage35. No significant difference map peaks appeared at susceptible sites such as disulfide bonds or acidic residues.

Ab initio phasing and automated structure completion

A central achievement of this work was solving the structure without a homologous model. Our workflow, conceptually similar to the fragment-based Fragon36 pipeline developed for X-ray data, began with molecular replacement in PHASER37 using a generic five-residue polyalanine helix. This yielded a low-scoring solution (TFZ=7.1) with a non-interpretable potential map (Fig. 2A, Supplementary Video 1); however, these initial phases were sufficient to bootstrap the dynamic density modification algorithm in ACORN38. This fragment-based phasing approach is similar to the strategies recently used to solve the structures of lysozyme and Proteinase K by MicroED20, similar to the ARCIMBOLDO39 and SHELXE40 based workflows. This approach resolved the phase ambiguity and produced an interpretable map covering the chain (Fig. 2B, Supplementary Video 2). The density-modified map was sufficient for BUCCANEER41 to automatically build 100% of the crambin model in a single pass. The final structure was refined with the applied twin model and ellipsoidal truncation to Rwork/Rfree values of 15.54% / 16.41%, yielding a model with excellent stereochemistry (Table 1). While these values are higher than typical X-ray structures at this resolution, they are characteristic of MicroED refinements where dynamical scattering effects are not fully modeled by standard kinematic refinement20. A hydrogen- and disorder-refined model is provided in the Supplementary Information (Supplementary Files); these coordinates are not used for Table 1 statistics. The maps from REFMAC resolve all non-hydrogen atoms and many hydrogen atoms, consistent with atomic resolution (Fig. 1F, Supplementary Fig. S5).

Positioning crambin among ab initio MicroED benchmarks

We compare this result with prior ab initio MicroED structures of triclinic lysozyme and proteinase K in Supplementary Table S4, summarizing resolution, completeness, R values, phasing fragments, microscope voltage, detector mode, and FIB use. Crambin complements these benchmarks as a sub-ångström, 200 kV, no-FIB, no energy-filter case with natural isoform heterogeneity. Representative overlays of electron potential, X-ray electron density, and neutron scattering-length maps are shown in Supplementary Fig. S5, highlighting complementary features. Crambin thus provides a useful reference point across modalities for electron-specific method development.

Crystal habit and implications for MicroED

The inversion of crystal quality, where X-ray-ideal blocks failed in MicroED while X-ray-unsuitable needles excelled, is rooted in the physical limitations of electron diffraction. The primary determinant for high-quality MicroED data is crystal thickness along the beam path, ideally below twice the inelastic mean free path (about 500–600 nm)30, to minimize dynamical scattering and absorption. While the block-like crystals possessed high internal order for X-rays, mechanically crushing them did not reliably produce fragments this thin; most remained too thick, degrading the electron diffraction. The spontaneously formed needles, however, were inherently thin in one dimension. When lying flat on the grid, they presented an ideal, electron-transparent path for the beam. This favorable habit introduces a severe preferred orientation. We directly overcame this challenge by using a serial crystallography approach, merging data from 58 crystals to build the necessary completeness.

Complementary chemical information in electron potential maps

Electron potential maps differ from X-ray electron-density and neutron scattering length density maps and can be sensitive to charge; hydrogen visibility is illustrated in Supplementary Fig. S549–52. We anticipate use of these data and maps for modeling electron scattering, hydrogen visualization, and charge-density analysis in future studies. This high-quality electron-based model, when combined with existing ultra-high-resolution X-ray and neutron data, including the 0.70 Å room-temperature solvent structure of crambin, creates an opportunity for joint and cross-modality refinement that can probe hydrogen bonding, protonation, and dynamic solvent organization in a single benchmark system26.

We determined the 0.85 Å ab initio MicroED structure of crambin directly from spontaneously formed nanocrystals obtained during ethanolic extraction. Data were collected at 200 kV without focused-ion-beam milling or an energy filter, and serial merging mitigated preferred orientation. Ellipsoidal truncation addressed anisotropy (Table 1; Supplementary Table S2). Using a minimal five-residue helical fragment and density modification, we obtained phases and automatically built the complete model (Fig. 2). Mixed PL/SI isoforms at residues 22 and 25 were refined as alternates with occupancies summing to 1, supported by omit-map evidence and an additional X-ray structure (Supplementary Files). Key statistics are reported in Table 1.
